classification.difficultyReason: Connect the amplitude formula to minimising its square, choose completing the square, and use a>b to recover the positive minimum.

content.prompt: Suppose that $a>b$. Show that the smallest possible amplitude of $(k+a)\cos x+(k+b)\sin x$ is $\dfrac{a-b}{\sqrt{2}}$.

answer.short:
$R_{\min}=\dfrac{a-b}{\sqrt{2}}$, attained when $k=-\dfrac{a+b}{2}$.

Complete the square in $R^2=(k+a)^2+(k+b)^2$.
answer.worked:
The amplitude is $R=\sqrt{(k+a)^2+(k+b)^2}$.

$$\begin{align*}R^2&=(k+a)^2+(k+b)^2\\R^2&=2k^2+2(a+b)k+a^2+b^2\\R^2&=2\left(k+\frac{a+b}{2}\right)^2+\frac{(a-b)^2}{2}\\R^2&\ge\frac{(a-b)^2}{2}.\end{align*}$$

Equality holds when $k=-\dfrac{a+b}{2}$. Since $a>b$,

$$\begin{align*}R_{\min}&=\sqrt{\frac{(a-b)^2}{2}}\\R_{\min}&=\frac{a-b}{\sqrt{2}}.\end{align*}$$
